results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

All 96 outline summaries match the controlling idea of their aligned spec paragraph, in spec order; the three opening callouts carry the thesis statement and match no paragraph. The Tool 4 example is summarised as 'bike frame size', but the draft's example is bike.battery_capacity_wh as the spec says: an outliner slip, not a mismatch.

Flagged two_ideas for p01, p14, p60, p81, p82 and the KEY POINTS callout: in each, the second idea is part of the spec's controlling idea for that unit (or is the callout's three-bullet thesis), so the unit holds one declared idea.

results.quote: Vertical mappings: Hearthly's "under offer" and "let agreed" map onto Reserved and Sold; Motorvane allows platform-set reservations only for dealers who opt in.
results.finding: The paragraph walks the Rotterdam bike through the table and then appends an unrelated sentence on vertical word mappings; the outliner marked two ideas. The spec places the mappings in p28's evidence, so the second idea comes from the spec; it belongs in the example lead-in (p27) or the rules list (p26).

Every unit traces to T1 (lookup, connection diagram, p05), T2 (each tool's purpose/use/template/example/mistakes/chapter), T3 (removal and incident paragraphs p28, p42, p49, p63, p71, p78) or T4 (conventions p02, register p92, conclusion).

Every table has a lead sentence naming what it records and every Veldmark example table is followed by an analysis or incident paragraph that states its point; Figure 1 has an explanatory caption; the two public sources in Tool 11 are each followed by what they show. Minor: the Tool 2 example lead names 'delete latency', which appears only inside the Listing lifetime row.

Every transition_in is realised at its boundary: the repeated tool labels (Use it when / The template / Veldmark example / Common mistakes / Learn more) carry the sequence, elaboration, example, contrast and additional_support relationships; the analysis and incident paragraphs open with explicit cause_effect or emphasis sentences ('The verdict follows from the scores', 'The contract replaces two incidents with two controls', 'The removal row is the one the Rotterdam bike tested', 'The two columns are the point of the card'); the conclusion opens with a summarising sentence.

results.draft_locus: Find the Template for the Question on Your Desk ¶2
results.finding: Reader A: 'This is out of place: at this point I had not seen Tool 11 or its rows, so the sentence meant nothing and I had to re-read it.' The organising principle both readers describe matches large_to_small with part order for the tools; this sentence is a footnote about a table row the reader has not met.
results.corroborated_by: reader-flow-b item 3 (Find the Template: 'This felt out of place. It is a footnote about a row in a table I had not yet seen.')

results.quote: the same phone number had registered a Motorvane private-seller account, and no field in the March process said who should tell Motorvane.
results.finding: Reader A: 'I had to re-read to connect this to the rollout row ... because the link between the phone number and the rollout gap is left implicit.' No phone number was mentioned before 'the same phone number', and the link to the rule never reaching other brands is left to the reader.
results.corroborated_by: reader-flow-b item 3 (Tool 8: 'I re-read "the same phone number" ... no phone number had been mentioned. "The March process" is also vague.')

results.quote: The records cite each other by identifier (`vm:tradeyard:nl:…`, `bike.frame_size_cm`, `POL-FRAUD-PAYLINK` v3, `listing.events.v1`, `pro-150@v5`, tenant `hl:es`)
results.finding: Reader A: 'Six identifiers arrive before any of the records or brands they belong to; on first read they were noise' and calls it 'the hardest sentence on the page for a first-time reader'. Reader B found the same list opaque but 'tolerable' as a summary.
results.corroborated_by: reader-flow-b item 3 (Opening blocks: 'Six opaque identifiers come before any of the tools that define them.')

results.quote: the lifecycle table, the SLA card and the event specification each force a named removal objective per consumer
results.finding: Reader A: 'When I got to Tool 3, the lifecycle table has no per-consumer removal objective ... so I went back to check whether I had misread the claim.' The lifecycle table derives behavior per state, not objectives per consumer.

results.quote: Seven of the twelve templates have a field for what happens when a listing ends: the lifecycle table, the feed contract, the SLA card, the index card, the enforcement card, the entitlement matrix and the event specification.
results.finding: Reader B: 'When I reached Tool 9 later, I had to look for that field. The matrix has no removal column ... I went back to check the claim.' The entitlement matrix template carries this only implicitly (Expire/Revoke ledger entries, a common mistake). Different template and passage from reader A's lifecycle-table point, so not counted as the same finding.

results.quote: Public cases show why the constraints row matters
results.finding: Reader A: 'the two external cases ... make this paragraph much longer than the other tools' "Use it when" lines; I lost the "when do I use this" thread inside it and had to come back to the first sentence.'

results.draft_locus: Tool 2: Vertical Requirement Profile and Share-Layer Row ¶5
results.quote: Stage gate for Motorvane on the shared ingestion engine: **feed success rate and delete latency no worse than Motorvane reports today.**
results.finding: Reader B: 'The row is about vehicle identity, but the stage gate is about Motorvane moving onto a shared ingestion engine, which is a different capability part. I could not tell whether the stage gate belongs to this row.'

results.quote: Each template leaves evidence someone else can check only while it stays true, above all in the fields that carry ownership, removal behavior and dates.
results.finding: Reader A: 'The sentence's construction made me re-read it to find the claim (templates must be kept true to be useful).' 'above all in the fields' attaches ambiguously.

Terms the flow readers met cold (Tradeyard, Motorvane, Hearthly, Keybridge, Femke's bike, the Essen Golf, Safe Deal, Ghost Inventory, Forced Fit, Search as System of Record, the effect projector, the advice forum, the consumer registry) belong to Veldmark, the failure-pattern names or the book's chapters, all in audience.already_knows. The does_not_know items (which record fits a decision, which fields are dropped first) are answered by the lookup table and the opening's ownership/removal/dates rule.
Opens with a direct statement of what the page is; no throat-clearing, dictionary or rhetorical-question opening.
The conclusion gives three habits with concrete incidents, not a restatement or a generic call to action.

Synthesises that templates leave checkable evidence only while kept true, that incident-derived fields (mass-change guard, send-time re-check, PublishRefused, group-urgent class) show how, and says what to do: review on a calendar, let incidents add fields, remove fields nobody reads.

'Each template leaves evidence someone else can check ... above all in the fields that carry ownership, removal behavior and dates' calls back to the opening's 'leaves evidence someone else can check' and 'keep the fields that carry ownership, removal behavior and dates'.

The intro reader gave the page order exactly as the roadmap promises: lookup table, diagram of how the records cite each other, twelve tools in part order with purpose/use/template/Veldmark example/three mistakes/chapter, then upkeep and sources, glossary and bibliography next. Its uncertainty is only the full list of the twelve, which the roadmap does not promise.

Reader answered (a) Tool 5 feed contract, listing-ingestion, absence_means plus the mass-change guard; (b) Tool 11 consolidation decision card, platform-consolidation, the gate behind each stage (with constraints and exit path as runners-up); (c) Tool 9 entitlement matrix, products-and-entitlements, billing basis and failure behavior. All three match the expected answers.

Reader named twelve working templates for the records Parts I to VIII ask a Chief Architect to keep, each with a Veldmark example, three common mistakes and its chapter; start with the record that changes the decision on your desk this week, fill only what changes it, write 'unknown'; keep templates as maintained data cited by one stable identifier; ownership, removal behavior and dates are dropped first. Matches expected.

Independent outline lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the spec's 96 paragraphs across intro, lookup, connect, twelve tools and conclusion; structure check confirms sections, unit counts and forms.
